back: n = 1.498; Abbe ≈ 58; SG ≈ 1.32. Thermosetting, cast-molded resin (allyl diglycol carbonate).
n = 1.586; Abbe ≈ 30; SG ≈ 1.20. Thermoplastic, injection molded, highest impact resistance, inherent UV blocking, needs a scratch coat.
n = 1.53; Abbe ≈ 43–45; SG ≈ 1.11 (lightest). Urethane-based, high impact resistance, excellent for drill mounts.
n = 1.523; Abbe ≈ 58–59; SG ≈ 2.54. Excellent scratch resistance and optics; heavy; must be tempered.
Index 1.60; Abbe roughly 36–42 depending on the monomer. Good compromise of thinness and optics.
Index 1.67; Abbe ≈ 32. Thinner than 1.60, more reflections (≈6.3% per surface uncoated).
Index 1.74; Abbe ≈ 33. Thinnest common plastic; reflects ≈7.3% per surface uncoated — AR strongly recommended.
Trivex 1.11 < poly 1.20 < CR-39 1.32 < high-index plastics ≈ 1.3–1.5 < crown glass 2.54.
Density of a material relative to water. Lens weight depends on SG and lens volume.
Thermoset (CR-39) cures permanently with heat and is cast. Thermoplastic (polycarbonate) softens with heat and is injection molded.
Polycarbonate and Trivex. Standard for children, sports, safety, and monocular patients.
5/8-inch steel ball (≈0.56 oz) dropped 50 inches onto the lens front surface (21 CFR 801.410).
Every glass lens is individually tested after tempering; plastic lenses may be batch tested by the manufacturer.
1/4-inch steel ball at 150 ft/s for high-impact safety eyewear.
Manufacturer's mark; high-impact lenses also carry a '+'.
Glass heated near softening, then cooled rapidly with air jets. Shows a strain pattern (e.g., Maltese cross) under polarized light.
Ion exchange in molten potassium nitrate: potassium ions replace sodium at the surface. Generally stronger than heat tempering; little visible strain pattern.
Surface curvature changes from center to edge. Allows flatter, thinner lenses with less magnification and fewer peripheral errors.
Different aspheric corrections in each principal meridian. Best for prescriptions with significant cylinder.
Lower the optical center 1 mm for every 2° of pantoscopic tilt.
FT-22, FT-25, FT-28 (most common), FT-35, FT-45 — the number is the seg width in mm.
One-piece, full-width segment with its optical center on the seg line: no image jump, wide near field, heavy ledge.
OC at the seg center (11 mm below top for a 22 mm seg); maximum image jump. Ultex A = 38 mm one-piece round seg.
Fused glass round bifocal: a higher-index glass button fused into a crown carrier.
Top of the seg at the lower eyelid margin.
Top of the seg at the lower edge of the pupil.
Intermediate depth (7 mm) × segment width (28 mm). Intermediate is usually 50% of the add.
Seg edge polished into a blur zone so no line is visible; no intermediate corridor.
(Distance PD − near PD) ÷ 2 per lens. Example: 64/60 → 2 mm per lens.
From the lowest point of the lens opening (lower bevel) to the seg line.
Seg drop = (B ÷ 2) − seg height when the seg top is below the datum line; above the datum it is a seg raise.

front: Segs fitted too high / too low
back: Too high: seg interferes with distance vision. Too low: patient must drop eyes or tip head back to read.
Flat-top seg at the bottom plus an inverted seg at the top for overhead near work (mechanics, electricians, librarians).
Different seg styles in each eye (different OC depths) to offset vertical imbalance at near.
Placed at the pupil center with monocular PDs and the patient in natural head posture.
Midway between the hidden engravings, usually a few mm below the fitting cross. Verify prism here.
Two permanent marks 34 mm apart (17 mm each side of the PRP). Add power usually below the temporal mark; logo below the nasal mark.
Distance power at the distance reference circle; add at the near circle or from the engraving.
Hard: wide clear zones, short corridor, steep astigmatism gradients. Soft: gentler gradients, narrower clear zones, easier adaptation.
Reaches full add in less vertical height; chosen for frames with small B dimensions.
Equal base-down prism in both PAL lenses to reduce thickness. No imbalance; verify at the PRP.
Peripheral cylinder on either side of the corridor caused by the changing surface curvature; increases with add power.
Near zone too low: patient must drop eyes or lift the chin to read. Too high: distance blur in straight-ahead gaze.
Find the engravings under bright light, dot them, align on the manufacturer's centration chart, then redraw the fitting cross, PRP, and circles.
Computer-controlled point-by-point surfacing; enables personalized and back-surface progressive designs.
Wide intermediate and near zones; power decreases toward the top. Not for driving.
Quarter-wave thin films cause destructive interference of reflected light; multilayers cover the visible spectrum.
√(n_lens). For n = 1.50 → ≈1.22. MgF₂ (≈1.38) is commonly used.
Uncoated CR-39 transmits ≈92%; a good AR coating raises it to about 99%.
Reduces reflections from light behind the wearer bouncing off the back of a dark lens into the eye.
Top layer that repels water and oils; keeps lenses cleaner and easier to clean.
Highly reflective front-surface film; reduces transmitted light and hides the eyes. Cosmetic; does not by itself ensure UV protection.
UV-C 100–280 nm; UV-B 280–315 nm; UV-A 315–380 nm (to 400 nm by some definitions).
Blocks essentially all radiation below 400 nm (all UV-B and UV-A).
Darker and slower to fade in the cold; lighter and faster to fade in the heat.
Windshields block most UV, so standard photochromics darken very little behind the windshield.
Vertical transmission axis blocks horizontally polarized glare from water, roads, and hoods. May black out some LCD displays.
Neutral: preserves natural color perception.
Enhances contrast; shifts colors warmer.
Absorbs blue; improves perceived contrast in haze, fog, or low light. Not a bright-sun tint.
Darkest at the top, lighter toward the bottom. Double gradient: dark top and bottom, lighter middle.
Tint density follows thickness: thick minus edges look darker. Plastics are surface-dyed and tint uniformly.
Reduces high-energy visible light ≈400–455 nm via absorbers (slight yellow cast) or reflective coatings (bluish reflection).
Creates base-up prism in the lower portion of the lens. Placed on the most minus (least plus) lens in the vertical meridian.
Base-down prism in the lower portion, usually molded plastic. Placed on the most plus (least minus) lens.
Equal to the vertical imbalance at the reading level. Consider when it reaches about 1.5Δ or more.
Faint horizontal line across the full lens at the level of the seg top.
Thin flexible vinyl with tiny prism ridges, applied to the back surface. Light and high-powered, but reduces acuity and contrast; temporary or diagnostic use.
Small central full-power aperture on a thin carrier. Reduces thickness and weight; limits the field.
Ring scotoma from strong edge prism in high-plus lenses; objects pop in and out of view.
High-minus lenticular: small central optical bowl with a flattened carrier margin to reduce edge thickness.
Small, round frame; frame PD close to patient PD; high-index material; AR coat; polished or rolled edges.

front: Frame PD wider than patient PD in minus lenses
back: Lenses are decentered nasally, making the temporal edges thicker.
MBS = ED + (2 × decentration per lens) + 2 mm. Decentration per lens = (frame PD − patient PD) ÷ 2.
